title: The School That Comes by Boat
paragraphs: During the monsoon season, many villages in northern Bangladesh are surrounded by water for months. Roads disappear, fields turn into lakes, and children who live on small islands of land cannot walk to school. For them, the solution is simple but unusual: the school comes to them, by boat.

Each morning, a long narrow boat painted bright blue glides to a different landing point. On its deck, a solar panel powers a few lamps and a laptop; inside, a long wooden bench seats thirty pupils, and there are a small library and a blackboard. The teacher, Shirin Akter, a twenty-six-year-old with a quiet voice and an extraordinary sense of direction, can steer the boat herself when the driver is ill.

Shirin knows the children's families personally. She is aware which ones have enough rice for the week and which ones do not, and she often arrives with extra books or a sack of lentils donated by a local charity. 'You cannot teach a hungry child fractions,' she says. 'First you listen. Then you teach.'

Lessons are flexible. When the water rises overnight, the boat starts earlier; when a wedding or a funeral takes place in a village, the class is moved to the afternoon. Some pupils come only three days a week because they must help their parents fish or harvest rice, so Shirin gives them short exercises to take home. Surprisingly, most of them return the exercises on time.

The project is not without difficulties. The boats are expensive to maintain, the funding depends on donations, and in the strongest storms, classes have to be cancelled for safety reasons. The charity that operates the school estimates that each boat costs several thousand taka a month in fuel and repairs, a sum that is hard to raise year after year.

Still, the results speak for themselves. Ten-year-old Rahim, who could not read a word two years ago, now reads aloud to his younger sister every evening. 'I want to be a doctor,' he says, then pauses and adds, 'or a boat driver.' Shirin smiles and, without looking up from her notebook, says that both jobs need patience. Their boat, meanwhile, is already moving toward the next landing.

title: Review: Seven Floors
paragraphs: At first glance, Seven Floors looks like every other apartment-block drama on television: a handful of neighbours, a few secrets and a lift that always seems to break down at the worst moment. Yet this Brazilian series, which finished its first season last month, is much cleverer than it appears, and it has quickly become one of the most discussed shows among my friends.

Each of the eight episodes is told from the point of view of a different resident. We begin with Dona Marlene, a retired seamstress who spends her days watching the street from her balcony, and move on to a teenage gamer, a nervous young doctor, a taxi driver who works nights and, finally, the building's manager, who turns out to know more than anyone suspects. The same events are shown again and again, but they change each time, like a sculpture seen from different sides.

This structure could easily have become repetitive, but the writers avoid the trap by giving every episode a different tone. The episode about the teenager is funny and fast; the one about the taxi driver is quiet and almost melancholy. The acting is consistently strong, particularly that of Lúcia Ferraz as Dona Marlene, whose face can express surprise, grief and mischief within a single scene.

The series also deserves credit for its restraint. There are no villains, only people who make understandable decisions with incomplete information. When a conflict is finally resolved, in the sixth episode, nobody is punished and nobody is entirely forgiven, which feels honest.

The weaknesses are few but noticeable. The final episode ties up too many loose ends too quickly, and one subplot about a missing cat is introduced and then abandoned. Some viewers may also find the pace slow, particularly in the opening episode, where the director seems to enjoy long shots of the corridors more than the plot requires.

Nevertheless, I recommend Seven Floors warmly. It is a modest series that trusts its audience to pay attention, and it rewards that trust with moments of real emotional force. Watch it with friends, because you will want to talk about it afterwards. And pay attention to the lift. It tells you more than you think.

title: Kings and Queens of the Park: An Interview
focus: Used to, would and reported speech
paragraphs: Every Saturday afternoon, in a corner of a park in Buenos Aires, thirty children sit around concrete chess tables. Their coach, Ernesto Villalba, seventy-four, spent forty years teaching mathematics before retiring. He agreed to talk to us between games.
Q: Why chess, and why in a park?

A: In the school where I taught, we had a chess club that was always empty. Children thought chess was for geniuses. So I decided to take a board outside, where a pensioner or two were already playing. Within a month, kids and old men were sharing tables, and everybody learned from everybody else.
Q: Do you need to be intelligent to play well?

A: No. You need to be patient. I've seen very clever pupils lose because they moved too fast, and slow, careful ones win because they thought about their opponent's idea. Chess punishes impatience more than it punishes stupidity. I once taught a boy of eight who, after losing a game, said, 'I lost because I didn't look.' I almost cried.
Q: What does chess teach beyond the game?

A: To accept consequences. In chess, you can't blame anybody else for a mistake, and you can't take back your move. At first, some children cry. Later they learn to shake hands, analyse what happened and try again. That's a lesson for life, much more than for chess.
Q: Do girls play as much as boys?
A: More every year. Last spring, the champion of our small tournament was a girl of nine who beat me twice, and I wasn't letting her win.
Q: Has the park changed?

A: A lot. When we started, we only had six boards, and we used to bring our own chairs from home. Then a neighbour donated some old pieces, and the local council painted the tables. Now we have a waiting list! I would never have imagined it.
Q: Do you have any plans?
A: I'd love to organise a tournament between parks across the city. Some people tell me I should rest at my age. I tell them that at my age the pieces move more slowly, but the ideas move faster.

title: What Maps Leave Out
paragraphs: Look at the world map in most classrooms, and you will see Greenland looking as big as Africa. It is a striking image, and a completely misleading one. In reality, Africa is much more than ten times larger. The map is not lying exactly; it is simply doing something that every flat map must do, which is to bend the truth.

The problem is geometrical. The Earth is a sphere, and a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing it, in the same way that an orange peel cannot be pressed flat without breaking. The most common solution, a sixteenth-century design by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, keeps directions accurate, which is excellent for sailors, but it enlarges areas as they approach the poles.

For navigation, this distortion did no harm. But as the map moved into schools and offices, it began to shape how people imagine the world. Countries near the equator, many of them in Africa, South America and South Asia, look smaller than they are, while Europe and North America seem larger and more central. It is hard to say how much this affects our opinions, but it is reasonable to think that images influence attitudes more than we realise.

Several alternatives exist. Some maps preserve the relative size of countries but have to twist their shapes; others present the world in an unusual orientation, with the south at the top. At first, these maps feel strange and even wrong, which is precisely the point. They remind us that our idea of 'up' and 'centre' is a convention, not a law of nature.

Does it matter? A sceptic might reply that adults can easily remember that maps are imperfect. Perhaps so. But habits of vision are stubborn, and I suspect that many of us would be surprised by how often we trust a drawing simply because it is neat and familiar.

The lesson goes beyond geography. Every summary, every chart and every headline is also a flat version of something more complicated, and every one of them has to stretch some part of reality in order to fit the page. The wise reader, like the wise traveller, asks a simple question: what has been left out, and what has been enlarged?

title: The Substitute
paragraphs: The class had made a substitute teacher cry every week that term, so when Mr Brenes walked in on Monday morning, carrying nothing but a worn leather bag and a smile, the students of 10B exchanged looks of quiet satisfaction. 'Another victim,' someone whispered. By the end of the first minute, three phones were out, and a paper plane was crossing the room.

Mr Brenes said nothing. He placed his bag on the desk, took out a small brass bell and rang it once. The sound was so clear and so unexpected that the room fell silent. 'Good morning,' he said. 'I'm told you are the most difficult class in the school. I would like to test that theory.'

Then he told them a story. A very short one, about a lighthouse keeper who lost his boat in a storm and had to learn to talk to the sea. It lasted five minutes. At the end, he stopped in the middle of a sentence and said, 'I'll tell you how it ends tomorrow, if you're all in your seats on time.' Then he handed out the exercises left by the regular teacher, and nobody complained.

The next day, every student was in their seat before the bell. Marisol Cruz, who usually arrived twenty minutes late, was the first. Mr Brenes finished the story, which ended badly for the lighthouse keeper and very well for the sea, and asked them to write their own endings. Some wrote funny ones, some wrote sad ones, and Dario, who had never completed a written task that term, filled four pages.

On Friday, Mr Brenes said goodbye. The regular teacher, Ms Solano, was coming back from her sick leave. The students were unusually quiet. 'Will you come again?' asked Dario, suddenly shy. 'If they ask me,' said Mr Brenes. 'But you don't need me. You only needed someone to bet that you could be quiet for five minutes.'

When Ms Solano returned, she found the room tidy, the homework done and, on the board, a message in an unfamiliar handwriting: 'Ask them about the lighthouse.' She did. Twenty-six hands went up at once. It took her a week to discover who had written the message, and a good deal longer to forgive herself for having doubted them.

title: Maré Youth Orchestra: Annual Report
paragraphs: ## Summary

This report reviews the activities of the Maré Youth Orchestra, a community music project in Salvador, Brazil, during its second full year. The orchestra has forty-two members aged between ten and nineteen and is supported by donations, a small city grant and ticket sales.
## Activities

During the year, the orchestra gave nine public concerts, including two in local schools and one in a hospital. A weekly rehearsal was held every Saturday morning, and smaller groups of players met on Wednesdays for individual coaching. In August, thirty members took part in a three-day music camp in the countryside, where they worked with two visiting teachers.
## Results

Membership grew from 31 to 42, an increase of roughly one third. Attendance at rehearsals averaged 87 per cent, compared with 74 per cent the previous year. A survey of members' parents indicated that 90 per cent felt that their children had become more disciplined and confident. Concert audiences totalled about 2,400 people. The oboe and the double bass remain the hardest positions to fill.
## Finances

Total income was 96,000 reais: 52,000 from donations, 30,000 from the city grant and 14,000 from tickets and sales. Expenses were 91,000 reais, mostly on teachers' fees (45,000), instrument repairs (28,000) and transport (18,000). The surplus of 5,000 reais will be placed in a fund for new instruments.
## Challenges

Despite these achievements, the orchestra has a waiting list of 23 children and lacks enough instruments for them. The roof of the rehearsal hall leaks in the rainy season, which has already forced the cancellation of three rehearsals. Volunteer teachers also leave frequently, since they have to combine rehearsals with other jobs.
## Goals for next year
The orchestra aims to buy ten additional instruments, repair the roof and begin a beginners' programme for twenty children on the waiting list.

title: A Proposal for Touch Tours
paragraphs: Dear Dr Montes,

I am writing to propose a new activity for the Museo del Valle: a monthly guided tour designed especially for blind and partially sighted visitors. I am a nineteen-year-old volunteer guide at the museum, and I have been inspired by a conversation with a visitor, Mr Gerardo Núñez, who told me last month that he had not visited a museum since he was a child.

At present, every exhibit is accompanied only by a written label and a visual display, which means that people who cannot see are largely excluded. This is a missed opportunity, since many objects in our collection, such as fossils, rock samples and sculptures, can be explored through touch. With careful preparation, a guide could describe each piece and allow visitors to handle replicas or selected originals.

I have discussed the idea with the city's Association of the Blind, which has kindly offered to train our volunteers free of charge. They have also suggested that tours should be limited to six participants, so that each person can touch and ask questions without feeling rushed. Additionally, I propose that the tours take place on a Monday morning, when the museum is closed to the general public and the rooms are quiet.

The cost would be low. I estimate that producing six replicas and printing descriptions in Braille would require about 8,000 pesos initially, and I am confident that this sum could be raised through a small fundraising event among the volunteers.

I appreciate that the museum already faces many demands, and that this proposal would add to the workload of the staff. However, I believe that it would strengthen the museum's reputation and show that it truly welcomes everybody. If you consider the idea worthwhile, I would be glad to prepare a more detailed plan and to present it to your team at a convenient time.
Thank you for your attention to this suggestion. I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours sincerely,
Paulina Ortega

title: In Praise of the Public Park
paragraphs: On Sunday afternoons, the park near my flat looks like a small, free festival. Families spread a blanket on the grass, teenagers practise dance steps for a video, a man sells coconut water from a cart, and two old friends argue over a chess board. Nobody asks for a ticket. I often think that if somebody invented this today, it would be considered a revolutionary social project.

Parks are public in the most important sense of the word: they belong to everyone, equally. In a city, where nearly every square metre has a price, that is remarkable. A park is one of the few places where a child from a crowded apartment can run without anyone charging for the space.

The benefits are well known, and fairly easy to believe. Green spaces make cities cooler in summer, absorb rainwater that would otherwise flood the streets, and offer homes to birds and insects. Children who grow up near green space also tend to play outdoors more, which no screen can replace. There is also a mental effect: most of us feel calmer after twenty minutes among trees, even if we cannot explain why.

Yet parks are surprisingly vulnerable. When a city needs money, a park, which produces no income, is an easy target. A plot of land that could host a shopping centre or a car park appears, to some officials, as a wasted opportunity. Little by little, benches are removed, lighting is neglected, and a neglected park becomes an unsafe one, which then 'proves' that it was not worth keeping.

I believe we should think about parks the way we think about schools and hospitals: as basic infrastructure, not as a luxury. That means regular funding, trained gardeners and, above all, the involvement of the people who use them. Neighbours who help to plan a park are far more likely to look after it. A few cities already invite residents to vote on park improvements, and the results are often modest but meaningful.

Next Sunday, I will go to my park again. I will bring a book, which I will probably not read, because there will be too many interesting things to watch. And I will remember that the best things in a city are not always the ones that can be bought.

title: Learning a Language Before It Is Lost
paragraphs: On Thursday evenings, in a small room above a bookshop in Mexico City, a group of teenagers repeat after their teacher: 'Niltze' (hello), 'Tlazohcamati' (thank you). Some of them struggle with the pronunciation; others laugh when they make mistakes. Nobody minds. The language they are learning, Nahuatl, has been spoken in what is now Mexico for many centuries.

The class, which is free, was started by Citlali Hernández, a twenty-two-year-old linguistics student whose grandmother speaks Nahuatl as her first language. 'My grandmother never taught my mother because, as a child, she was punished for speaking it at school,' Citlali explains. 'So my mother grew up with Spanish only. When I realised that the language could disappear with my grandmother, I felt I had to do something.'

Many students come from families with no connection to indigenous languages. Mauricio, sixteen, decided to sign up after learning that words he uses every day, such as 'tomato' and 'avocado', come from Nahuatl. 'It was like discovering a secret in my own kitchen,' he says. Others come out of curiosity about history, and a few, like Ximena, because they want to speak with their grandparents.

The lessons combine games, songs and short conversations. Students learn the names of animals and foods, then use them to invent small stories, which they perform for each other. Citlali avoids grammar rules at first, believing that confidence matters more than precision. 'If you are afraid of making a mistake, you'll never speak,' she says. 'Mistakes are how my grandmother and I understand each other.'

The project faces several challenges. There are few textbooks written for young people, and the available ones often use different spelling systems, which confuses a beginner. Citlali has started to write her own materials, with the help of her grandmother and two teachers from a nearby university. She also worries that a single weekly class is not enough to make anyone fluent.

Nevertheless, the results are encouraging. Last month, Ximena phoned her grandmother and greeted her in Nahuatl for the first time. According to Citlali, there was a long silence, and then her grandmother began to cry. 'They weren't sad tears,' she says. 'It was the sound of a language being welcomed home.'

options: She is moved when younger people speak her language
She refuses to speak Nahuatl
She teaches the class
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: al oír a Ximena saludar en náhuatl 'her grandmother began to cry', y Citlali aclara que no eran lágrimas tristes.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the different spelling systems?
options: To explain a difficulty for beginners
To describe how textbooks are printed
To criticise Citlali's teaching
questions.explain_es: Propósito: aparece en el párrafo de los desafíos, 'which confuses a beginner'.

questions.q: In 'Some of them struggle with the pronunciation', 'struggle with' means…
options: practise it for hours
find it difficult
improve it quickly
questions.explain_es: El contraste con 'others laugh when they make mistakes' indica que a algunos les cuesta la pronunciación.
